title: Modi Breaks Silence on Exam Crisis as India Youth Protests Escalate
excerpt: Prime Minister proposes special courts and pledges cabinet action as tens of thousands of young Indians demand the education minister's resignation over NEET paper leaks that affected 2 million students.
body:
• PM Modi proposed special fast-track courts to prosecute exam paper leakers — his first public response to the weeks-long crisis — but protesters rejected the offer as a "distraction."
  • The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, born from online satire in May, has grown into the biggest youth-led challenge to Modi's government since 2014, with tens of thousands converging on Delhi.
  • Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike after negotiations with two federal ministers, while CJP leaders agreed to formal talks with the government on Friday.
  • Protests have paralyzed central Delhi — shutting metro stations, cutting mobile internet, and forcing businesses to close — and spread to Mumbai, Pune, Kolkata, Bengaluru, and other cities.

Modi Responds After Weeks of Silence

Prime Minister Narendra Modi broke weeks of public silence on Thursday, proposing special courts to prosecute those behind national exam paper leaks and pledging that his cabinet would approve stricter anti-leak legislation at a meeting on Friday. "Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!" Modi posted on X, his first direct public statement since the crisis erupted.

https://x.com/BDUTT/status/2080225993470710016

The response came after the Cockroach Janta Party, a youth-led movement that started as an online joke in May, mobilized tens of thousands of protesters to march on parliament on Monday in defiance of a police ban. Officers fired tear gas and beat demonstrators with batons, injuring at least 180 people on both sides, according to Delhi Police and protest organizers, according to Reuters.

But the CJP swiftly dismissed Modi's proposal. "Dharmendra Pradhan Must Resign," the organization wrote on X in response. CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka pressed further: "Modi-ji, tell us why are paper leaks happening in this country in the first place? Fast-track courts are set up in this country for every other issue, but whether those fast-track courts have actually solved those issues — you know the answer to that question, and so do we."

From Online Satire to Mass Movement

The CJP traces its origins to a single post on X by Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old Boston University graduate and political communications strategist. On May 16, he wrote: "What if all cockroaches come together?" — a response to Supreme Court Justice Surya Kant's comments that many interpreted as likening unemployed youth to cockroaches, according to CNN.

What began as internet satire rapidly became a rallying point for millions of young Indians frustrated by chronic unemployment and systemic exam corruption. The immediate catalyst was the leak of NEET (National Eligibility cum Entrance Test) question papers in May, affecting some 2 million aspiring medical students and forcing a national re-examination. Local media have linked the leaks to about a dozen student suicides, according to Reuters.

The movement launched its first sit-in protest on June 6. Within weeks, it drew support from opposition parties, rights activists, and Bollywood stars including Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt, and Kareena Kapoor, who posted messages of solidarity on social media.

Delhi Paralyzed, Protests Spread Nationwide

Central Delhi has been effectively shut down. The Delhi Metro Rail Corp. closed up to 17 stations for the third time this week on Friday. Authorities blocked mobile internet in the protest zone, disrupting digital payments for shops and restaurants. The New Delhi Traders Association asked all businesses in the Connaught Place central business district to close early, citing security advisories, according to Reuters.

At the Jantar Mantar protest site — a 300-year-old observatory surrounded by open parkland that has become the movement's headquarters — more than 10,000 demonstrators gathered on Wednesday night despite monsoon rains. Fresh clashes erupted, with some protesters throwing stones and bottles at police, who responded with tear gas and cane charges.

"It has been 25 days so far. Even if it takes 25 months, that is acceptable, but we will not move from here."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP founder

Protests have spread beyond the capital to Mumbai, Pune, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Ranchi, Thiruvananthapuram, and Jammu, according to local media and Reuters.

Wangchuk Ends Fast, Talks Set for Friday

Prominent activist Sonam Wangchuk, 59, ended a 26-day hunger strike overnight after negotiations with two federal ministers. Wangchuk said on X that he broke his fast "at the urging of scores of members of parliament and following a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country." He promised to release details of the talks in a forthcoming video, according to Reuters.

Modi responded by urging Wangchuk to follow doctors' advice and "regain weight lost" during the fast. CJP founder Dipke thanked Wangchuk for his "courage and sacrifice" but made clear the movement would not stand down. "We won't let Sonam sir's sacrifice go in vain," he said.

CJP leaders agreed to meet government ministers at a neutral venue on Friday for formal talks. "We hope that the government comes with an open mind and it will listen to the people of this country who have been out on the roads for so long," CJP spokesperson Saurav Das told reporters. He added: "We are not backing out."

Opposition Seizes the Moment

The crisis has handed opposition parties a rare opening against Modi's BJP, which counts young voters as a core constituency. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi staged a sit-in outside Modi's residence on Tuesday and was briefly detained by police along with his sister Priyanka Vadra and other senior party leaders, according to Reuters.

"An attack on students is an attack on every Indian family," Gandhi said. "PM Modi believes he can get away without answers, without consequences. He cannot. Not this time."

Opposition lawmakers disrupted the monsoon session of parliament this week, forcing a temporary suspension of proceedings and demanding a debate on both the exam leaks and police violence against protesters.

Education Minister Pradhan, who last month called the CJP the "B-team of terror groups," offered his first conciliatory remarks late Tuesday, saying the government was committed to addressing concerns and reforming the exam system, according to CNN.

What Comes Next

The federal cabinet meets Friday to finalize draft legislation toughening penalties for exam fraud, with Modi promising parliamentary approval "at the earliest." But the CJP has made clear that legislative fixes alone will not end the standoff — they want structural reform to prevent leaks, not just harsher punishment after they occur.

For the Indian diaspora, the crisis underscores long-standing anxieties about the integrity of competitive exams that serve as the gateway to professional careers. NEET is among the most consequential exams for Indian families worldwide, and the leaks have shaken faith in a system that millions depend on to build their futures.

Whether Friday's talks produce a breakthrough or simply buy time may determine whether India's Gen Z protest movement — now the biggest street challenge to Modi's government in over a decade — marks a turning point or settles into a prolonged standoff with the state.
nri_angle: The NEET exam crisis directly impacts millions of Indian diaspora families who invest heavily in competitive exam preparation as a pathway to professional careers.
